title: The Party
concept: After this one you can name the six things people do with an hour, and you can tell real talk from small talk in a crowded room.
bookIdea: People fill their time together in six ways: withdrawal, rituals, pastimes, work, games and intimacy. Real intimacy is the rarest, and most social contact takes the form of games.
bookSource: Games People Play, Introduction and ch. 3 to 5; Scripts People Live, ch. 1; TA Today, ch. 9

opener.setting: Friday, 19:30. A brewery near the station. Halden's monthly, and Sam came as your plus-one.

lines.cue: hand on your back at the door
six corners of the room, and nobody has waved yet

opener.ask: Which corner of this room has real talk in it, and which one only sounds like it?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Three lines from the week. Tap what the people in them were doing with that hour.

items.text: “Did you see the match last night?” “Only the second half. Their defence is a joke.”
items.why: Small talk. It is one shared topic with a couple of easy lines each, and little is at stake. That safety is the point of it.

traps.0: Alone would mean nobody is talking. Two people are talking, so the hour isn't alone.
traps.2: Real would mean something true was said. Nothing true was said here, which is why it is safe.

items.example:
A school bus stop.
“They've put the fares up again.” “Don't I know it. It was cheaper last year.”
Two lines on one topic, little at stake, and both of you are glad of them.

items.text: “I haven't told anyone this. Not even my closest friend.”
items.cue: a quiet corner, not looking at you
items.why: Real. Something true was said, and it can't be joked away. Real talk is rare because something can happen in it.

traps.0: Trap would need a hook and a sting. Nobody is being used here, so calling it a trap gets it wrong.
traps.2: Work would be about the job. This is about her, and she didn't say it for the team.

items.example:
A family dinner, late.
“I got the letter. I didn't tell Dad.”
Nobody needs to answer fast. The table goes quiet, and that quiet is the point.

items.text: “Can you review the PR before standup?”
items.cue: not looking up from his screen
items.why: Work. It is about getting something done, and it has a deadline in it.

traps.1: Routine is the same words every time, like a Monday update. This is a one-off request about one PR.
traps.2: Trap would be a hook with a sting in it. A review request is just a request, unless it has been dressed up.

items.example:
A school group project.
“Can you send your part before Friday?”
It has a task and a date, so it is work, not a hook.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Six corners of the room. Put each one in its bin, then choose where you go.

items.prompt: Six corners of the room. For each one, what are people doing with that hour?

items.text:
Near the door, Daniel and the CFO:
“Good turnout.”
“Better than last month.”
“The Q3 numbers. Monday, Monday.”
items.why: The same words as last month's party. Routine fills the hour and asks nothing back.

items.text:
The long table, Clara and three interns:
“What are you paying near the station?”
“Up again for a one-bedroom, can you believe it.”
“It's worse by the bus stop now.”
items.why: Rent prices. Safe and pleasant, and it goes nowhere. Small talk keeps the room friendly.

items.text:
The corner booth, two engineers and a laptop:
“If we batch the writes…”
“Then the retry logic breaks.”
“Okay, show me the logs.”
items.why: It is work talk about batching and retries, and it ends with a job to do.

items.text:
The balcony, two people close together:
“...I didn't tell anyone that before.”
“I'm glad you told me.”
Quiet. Nobody else is out there.
items.why: Something true was said, and someone was glad to hear it. Real talk is rare because something can happen in it.

items.text:
The bar, Sam and a stranger:
“Have one with me, come on, you're on holiday.”
“I'm driving…”
“One. For me.”
items.why: “One. For me.” is a hook. The offer sounds kind, and the cost arrives later, when the evening is gone.

items.text:
A stool by the wall, Omar:
Phone face-up, back to the room.
Nobody has spoken to him in twenty minutes.
items.why: His back is to the room and his phone is up. The hour is spent alone, even in a crowd.

items.example:
A train carriage on a long ride.
Most people have their earphones in. Two friends are chatting, and one person stares at the window.
Each is spending the same hour in a different way.

items.title: Friday, 19:30, the brewery near the station
items.setting: Halden's monthly. Sam came as your plus-one, and you have a drink in your hand.

lines.text: Sit at Clara's table and ask about rent.
lines.outcome: Twenty minutes of rent prices. Pleasant, and nothing happens. Clara, at some point: “We should actually talk sometime.”
lines.why: Small talk is safe because little can happen in it. You get a warm nod with almost no risk, and that is the trade.

lines.text: Walk out to the balcony and join the two quiet people.
lines.outcome: They stop talking. The woman looks at her drink, and the moment is gone.
lines.why: Real talk is private, so you can't join it by stepping in. Only an invitation gets you in.

lines.text: Go over to Omar and say “Hey.”
lines.outcome: “Hey.” “Hey.” He goes back to his phone, with his back to the room.
lines.why: Alone, even in a crowd. One hello is polite, and it leaves Omar on his phone, so the hour stays his.

lines.text: Sit by the wall with Omar and say nothing for ten seconds.
lines.outcome: After a while, Omar: “Back's killing me. Hate these things.”
lines.why: Silence can be company. He spoke because nothing was asked of him, and what he said was true.

beats.cue: ten minutes on, the room still loud. Where now?

lines.text: Walk over to Daniel and the CFO.
lines.outcome: “Good you came.” Then he turns back to the CFO, and the Q3 numbers take over the talk.
lines.why: Routine. “Good you came” is the line Daniel gives every month, so it fills the hour and asks nothing back.

lines.text: Go to the bar, where Sam is holding a drink out for you.
lines.outcome: “Good man,” Sam says, and orders you another.
lines.why: A drink handed across a bar feels like being included, and it costs you your clear head for the evening. The hook is in the offer.

lines.text: Go to the bar and turn the drink down. “I'm good, I'll grab a water.”
lines.outcome: “Boring!” Sam calls across the bar, and he laughs anyway. You get your water.
lines.why: A clear no, said lightly, with no lecture in it. It costs a little of Sam's warmth, and it keeps your head clear for the evening.

beats.text: “You're alright, you know. Maya said you'd be boring.”
beats.cue: in the cab at 23:10, window down, a bit drunk

lines.text: “Thanks, Sam. I'm glad you're having a good time.”
lines.outcome: “Yeah? Okay. Okay.” He leans his head on the window.
lines.why: He gave a warm nod wrapped around a cold one, the boring bit. Taking the warm part and leaving the jab alone keeps it clean.

lines.outcome: He laughs, then looks out at the road. “Fair.”
lines.why: A joke back is a warm nod too, and it lands on the fun part of what he said.

lines.outcome: “She does.” He stares at the road for the rest of the ride.
lines.why: It turns his nod into a jab at Maya. He offered something warm, and you handed it back as a dig.

beats.text: “Night, roommate. One for the road? I've got a bottle.”
beats.cue: the flat door, just before midnight

lines.outcome: “Night, boring,” he says, and goes in grinning.
lines.why: A clear no, said kindly, still leaves him a nod. You didn't have to explain, and you didn't have to take the bottle.

lines.outcome: He pours two. Tomorrow's going to be a long one.
lines.why: Yes to the bottle is the same hook again. He gets company, and you pay for the morning.

lines.outcome: “Deal,” he says, and misses the door handle twice.
lines.why: A promise for later keeps the door open without a drink in your hand. It is a warm answer, though a blurred one.

items.example:
A cousin's engagement party.
Three people talk about the venue. One person sits alone by the cake, and one couple whispers in the garden.
Nobody is wrong to be where they are.

items.text: The balcony looked like small talk, and it was real. Why couldn't you just walk in and join it?
options: Real talk is private, so you can only be invited into it
You walked in without a topic, so they had nothing to answer
Length of acquaintance decides who gets asked in
items.why: Real talk is private, and it is rare because something can happen in it. You don't join it by stepping in. Someone has to ask you in.

traps.1: A topic is what gets you into small talk, because small talk runs on one subject at a time. The balcony was not small talk, so a better opener would still have broken in on something private.
traps.2: Years of knowing someone does not, by itself, get you into a private moment. You could know them well and still not be asked in.

items.example:
A wedding reception.
Two cousins whisper by the window.
You walk over, and they stop. That talk was theirs, and you wait to be asked.

debrief.nadia: There are six things people do with an hour: alone, routine, small talk, work, trap and real. Real talk is the rarest of the six. The balcony looked like small talk, but it was real, and real talk can only be invited into. Small talk is safe because little can happen in it, and real talk is rare because something can.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this time structuring: the six ways people fill their time together are withdrawal, rituals, pastimes, work, games and intimacy. Berne says intimacy is rare and that most social contact takes the form of games.

reflection.prompt: Think of your last evening with other people. Which of the six things took most of the hours, and was there one hour that felt real?
